plan: Literary narrative of about 640 words (CLD-P-ACT-R-000025) about a violinist placed second chair; structure, point of view and figurative-language items to vary subskills; one hard item (ending). Plus R024-07 resubmitted on CLD-P-ACT-R-000024.

passages.title: Second Chair
passages.text:
Nadia found out from the list taped to the band-room door, the way everyone at Westbrook High found out everything. First violin, first chair: Lucy Han. Second chair: Nadia Osei. She read it twice, as though the names might trade places if she gave them time, then went to her locker and stood in front of it without opening it.

She and Lucy had shared a music stand for two years. Lucy was the one who counted under her breath, who forgot her rosin, who once played an entire rehearsal with her shoe untied because she had not noticed. Nadia was the one who noticed things. She had assumed—she could see now that she had assumed—that noticing was the same as leading.

The spring concert was three weeks away. Second chair turns the pages. It is a small job, and everyone in the section knows exactly how small. At the first rehearsal Nadia turned the pages a beat late, then a beat early, and once so hard that the page tore along the binding. Lucy taped it back together without a word.

"You can just say it," Nadia told her afterward, in the parking lot.
"Say what?"
"That I'm being a baby."
Lucy shifted her case to her other hand. "I was going to say you turn pages like you're mad at them." She waited, and when Nadia did not laugh, she added, "Mr. Ferrante said it was close. He said the audition came down to the slow movement."
"That's supposed to help?"
"No," Lucy said. "It's just true."

That night Nadia played the slow movement alone in her room, recorded it on her phone, and listened back with her eyes closed. She had always thought of that movement as the easy part: long notes, nothing fast. On the recording the long notes sagged in the middle, like a rope held by people who had stopped paying attention. She played it again, and again. By eleven o'clock the notes held their shape, mostly, and she understood, without enjoying the understanding, what Mr. Ferrante had heard.

At the concert she turned every page exactly on time. Halfway through the slow movement, Lucy's note slipped flat, a small sour sag that probably no one in the audience could have named. Nadia heard it at once. Without looking up, she eased her own note down to meet it, so that for two bars the stand sounded like one instrument slightly out of tune instead of two instruments arguing. Lucy glanced at her, then back at the music.

Afterward Lucy found her by the coat racks. "You covered for me," she said.
"I noticed," Nadia said. It was not quite an answer, but Lucy seemed to take it as one, and for the first time in three weeks Nadia found that she did not mind being the one who noticed.

passages.title: The Year Without a Summer
passages.text:
In April 1815, Mount Tambora, a volcano on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, erupted with a force that dwarfed anything in recorded history. The explosion killed thousands of people on the island and in the surrounding seas, and it hurled ash and gas high into the atmosphere. Then, for a time, nothing unusual seemed to happen elsewhere in the world. The strangest consequences arrived more than a year later and half a planet away.

The eruption had injected enormous amounts of sulfur gas into the stratosphere, well above the level where rain could wash it out. There the gas formed a thin haze of tiny droplets that spread around the globe and reflected part of the incoming sunlight back into space. The cooling it caused was modest when averaged over the whole Northern Hemisphere, less than one degree Celsius. But averages can hide a great deal.

In New England, snow fell in June 1816, and hard frosts returned in July and August, killing corn and other crops just as they began to ripen. In parts of Europe, cold, relentless rain rotted the harvest in the fields. Grain prices soared, and in some regions food riots broke out. Farmers who had never thought about the upper atmosphere found their year ruined by it. Few people in Europe or North America had even heard of the eruption, and no one yet understood how a volcano could change the weather an ocean away; many blamed sunspots, or simply bad luck.

The year 1816 came to be called the Year Without a Summer, and it shows something that a single average figure cannot. A small drop in mean temperature matters less than when the cold arrives. A few unseasonable frosts in the middle of the growing season can destroy a crop that would have survived a winter several degrees colder than usual.

The cold summer also left a cultural trace. Kept indoors by storms at a villa near Lake Geneva, a group of young English writers held a contest to see who could write the most frightening story, and Mary Shelley began the novel that became Frankenstein. It is tempting to say that the volcano produced the novel, and the story is often told that way. It would be more accurate to say that the weather supplied the occasion; the ideas were already Shelley's own.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the way the passage is organized?

choices.A: It opens at the concert and then flashes back to explain how the main character came to lose her position.
choices.B: It moves from a disappointing announcement, through private practice, to a public moment that changes how the main character feels.
choices.C: It presents a series of rehearsals in which the main character gradually overtakes her rival and wins back her place.
choices.D: It moves from a talk with a teacher to a performance that proves the teacher's original judgment wrong.

candidates.evidence: Nadia found out from the list taped to the band-room door
candidates.explanation: The story begins with the posted list, follows Nadia's rehearsal and her practice at home, and ends at the concert, where covering Lucy's note changes how Nadia feels about her role.

A.rationale: The story is told in order; the concert comes near the end.

C.rationale: Nadia never overtakes Lucy, and only one rehearsal is described.

D.rationale: Nadia never talks with Mr. Ferrante, and her practice suggests his judgment was sound.

hints: Put the main events in the order they happen.

strategy.explanation: List the scenes in order, then match.

candidates.remember: Structure questions ask about the order and kind of scenes.

candidates.stem: The statement in paragraph 2 that Nadia "had assumed—she could see now that she had assumed—that noticing was the same as leading" mainly suggests that Nadia:

choices.A: had always resented how careless Lucy was during rehearsals.
choices.B: had known for some time that Lucy was the stronger player.
choices.C: had never wanted the responsibility of leading the section.
choices.D: had believed her attentiveness made her the natural choice to lead.

candidates.evidence: She had assumed—she could see now that she had assumed—that noticing was the same as leading.
candidates.explanation: Nadia thought that being the one who noticed things meant she would lead; the repeated "she had assumed" shows she now sees that belief was mistaken.

A.rationale: The details about Lucy are affectionate, and resentment is never stated.

B.rationale: The repetition shows she is only now seeing her assumption.

C.rationale: She is upset at losing first chair, so she did want it.

hints: What did Nadia think her noticing would earn her?
candidates.remember: A repeated phrase often marks a realization.

candidates.stem: In paragraph 3, the detail that Lucy "taped it back together without a word" mainly serves to:

choices.A: show that Lucy is angry with Nadia but is unwilling to say so out loud.
choices.B: suggest that Lucy did not notice that the page had been torn at all.
choices.C: contrast Lucy's calm with the frustration Nadia shows in turning the pages.
choices.D: reveal that Lucy has torn pages in the same way in the past.

candidates.evidence: Lucy taped it back together without a word.
candidates.explanation: Nadia turns the pages so hard that one tears; Lucy calmly repairs it without comment, so the detail sets Nadia's frustration against Lucy's restraint.

A.rationale: Nothing suggests anger; her later words are friendly and direct.

B.rationale: She tapes it, so she noticed.

hints: How does Lucy react compared with how Nadia is acting?

strategy.explanation: Compare the two characters' actions in paragraph 3.

candidates.remember: Small actions can reveal character by contrast.

candidates.stem: When Lucy says, "No . . . It's just true," she is most likely:

choices.A: making fun of Nadia for being upset about the results.
choices.B: giving Nadia honest information rather than trying to comfort her.
choices.C: admitting that she does not believe she deserved first chair.
choices.D: hinting that Mr. Ferrante might change his decision.

candidates.explanation: Nadia asks whether the information is meant to help; Lucy says no, it is simply true, so she is being honest rather than consoling.

A.rationale: Her tone is plain, not mocking, and she offers real information.

C.rationale: She reports the teacher's view; she does not doubt the result.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests the decision could change.

strategy.explanation: Read the two lines before Lucy's reply.

candidates.remember: Read a line of dialogue as an answer to the line before it.

candidates.stem: The comparison of the long notes to "a rope held by people who had stopped paying attention" mainly suggests that the notes:

choices.A: were played too loudly for a quiet, slow movement.
choices.B: ended too soon because Nadia was rushing through them.
choices.C: clashed with the notes Lucy was playing beside her.
choices.D: lost steadiness because Nadia's focus slipped while she held them.

candidates.evidence: the long notes sagged in the middle, like a rope held by people who had stopped paying attention
candidates.explanation: A rope sags when the people holding it stop paying attention; the image suggests the long notes lost tension in the middle because Nadia's attention lapsed.

B.rationale: The notes "sagged in the middle"; they did not end early.

C.rationale: Nadia is practicing alone in her room.

hints: What happens to a rope when the people holding it stop paying attention?

strategy.explanation: Picture the image, then match it to the notes.

candidates.remember: Ask what the image and the thing it describes share.

candidates.stem: Nadia lowers her own note during the concert most likely in order to:

choices.A: signal to Lucy that she should retune her violin.
choices.B: correct a habit of playing sharp that she noticed while practicing.
choices.C: match Lucy's flat note so that the mistake is harder to hear.
choices.D: make sure the audience can tell that Lucy has made a mistake.

candidates.evidence: she eased her own note down to meet it
candidates.explanation: She lowers her note "to meet" Lucy's flat note, so the two sound "like one instrument" instead of clashing: she is covering Lucy's mistake.

A.rationale: She does it "without looking up" and keeps playing; it is not a signal.

B.rationale: Her practice revealed sagging notes, not sharp ones.

D.rationale: She does the opposite: the stand sounds like one instrument.

hints: What does "to meet it" refer to?
candidates.remember: Read for the stated result of an action.

candidates.subskill: Connecting the ending to earlier events
candidates.stem: The last sentence of the passage most strongly suggests that Nadia:

choices.A: sees her attentiveness as a strength in its own right, not a poor substitute for leading.
choices.B: has decided, after saving the performance, that she deserved first chair after all.
choices.C: still resents being second chair but has decided to hide that from Lucy.
choices.D: plans to audition again next year so that she can replace Lucy.

candidates.evidence: Nadia found that she did not mind being the one who noticed
candidates.explanation: Earlier she had thought noticing was the same as leading; now noticing has let her help Lucy, and she is at peace with that role. B overreads her success; C contradicts the text.

B.rationale: She saved the moment, but the passage never suggests she now thinks the result was wrong; her practice confirmed it.

C.rationale: The sentence says she "did not mind" being the one who noticed.

hints: How does Nadia feel about "being the one who noticed" at the start compared with the end?

strategy.explanation: Rule out choices that contradict the last sentence or go beyond it.

candidates.remember: Endings often answer an idea raised early in a story.

author_checklist.hardness: Choice B is tempting because Nadia does save the performance, but the passage has already shown, through her practice, that the decision was sound; students must connect the ending to paragraph 2's realization.

candidates.stem: The story is told from the point of view of:

choices.A: Nadia, who describes the events in her own words.
choices.B: Lucy, who describes how Nadia reacted to losing.
choices.C: a narrator who reveals the thoughts of every character equally.
choices.D: a narrator who reveals Nadia's thoughts but not Lucy's.

candidates.evidence: she understood, without enjoying the understanding, what Mr. Ferrante had heard
candidates.explanation: The narrator refers to both girls as "she" but reports only Nadia's inner thoughts, such as what she assumed and understood.

A.rationale: Nadia is called "she"; the narrator is not Nadia.

B.rationale: Lucy is also referred to in the third person.

C.rationale: Only Nadia's thoughts are given; Lucy's are shown only through what she says and does.

hints: Whose thoughts does the narrator tell you directly?

strategy.explanation: Check pronouns, then check whose thoughts are reported.

candidates.remember: Third-person narrators can still stay close to one character.

candidates.stem: The final paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: return to the science of the eruption and summarize it.
choices.B: prove that bad weather is necessary for great literature.
choices.C: explain why food riots broke out in Europe.
choices.D: add a cultural consequence and qualify a popular claim about it.

candidates.evidence: The cold summer also left a cultural trace.
candidates.explanation: The paragraph adds a cultural consequence (the writing contest) and then qualifies the claim that the volcano produced the novel.

A.rationale: The final paragraph discusses a novel, not the science.

B.rationale: The author makes no such general claim.

hints: What new kind of consequence does the last paragraph introduce?

strategy.explanation: Look at the paragraph's first and last sentences.

candidates.remember: Closing paragraphs often widen the scope or qualify a claim.
